title: n8n Advanced: Expressions, HTTP Request, and the Code Node
summary: This day unlocks n8n's real power and starts bridging you from pure no-code to low-code, which is exactly the growth an automation engineer needs. Expressions are n8n's way of dynamically referencing data - instead of typing a fixed value, you write
content:
# n8n Advanced: Expressions, HTTP Request, and the Code Node ##### The integration that does not exist Sooner or later, every automation engineer hits this wall. A client uses a niche tool — a regional payment gateway, an Indian GST filing service, an internal inventory system built by a contractor in 2019. You search the integrations list. Nothing. In a pure no-code tool, the project stops here. In n8n, you shrug, open the app's API docs, drop in an **HTTP Request** node, and carry on. Ten minutes later the "unsupported" app is fully integrated. That is what today is about: the three features — **expressions**, the **HTTP Request node**, and the **Code node** — that take you from *"I can use the tools someone built for me"* to *"I can integrate anything."* This is the low-code transition, and industry reviews of low-code platforms (Sahay et al., 2020) consistently identify this escape hatch as the difference between platforms that scale with a team and platforms that get abandoned. ##### Expressions: referencing data dynamically Every parameter box in n8n has a toggle: **Fixed** or **Expression**. Fixed means the literal text you typed. Expression means "evaluate this at run time." Expressions use `{{ }}` and JavaScript inside. The core objects: ```javascript {{ $json.email }} // a field from the current item {{ $json.customer.contact.email }} // nested path {{ $json.items[0].sku }} // array element {{ $('Webhook').item.json.order_id }} // a field from a named earlier node {{ $('Set Fields').all() }} // every item from a named node {{ $now.format('dd LLL yyyy') }} // current time (Luxon DateTime) {{ $execution.id }} // this run's ID {{ $workflow.name }} // workflow metadata ``` Because it is real JavaScript, you can compute inline rather than adding a node: ```javascript {{ $json.name.trim().toUpperCase() }} {{ $json.items.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.price * i.qty, 0) }} {{ $json.email.includes('@') ? 'valid' : 'invalid' }} {{ ($json.phone || '').replace(/\D/g, '') }} {{ $json.tags?.join(', ') ?? 'none' }} ``` Two habits will save you hours. First, use the **Schema view** in the INPUT panel and *drag* fields into parameter boxes — n8n writes the correct expression for you, eliminating typos in nested paths. Second, hover over any expression: n8n shows a live preview of the evaluated result using the current input data. If the preview says `undefined`, your path is wrong, and you know immediately rather than after a failed run. The `?.` (optional chaining) and `??` (nullish coalescing) operators in that last example are worth adopting as defaults. `$json.customer.email` throws an error if `customer` is missing; `$json.customer?.email ?? 'unknown'` quietly returns a fallback. Optional fields are the norm in real payloads. ##### The HTTP Request node: your universal adapter This single node can talk to any REST API on the internet. Its configuration mirrors exactly the request anatomy you learned on Day 3 — method, URL, query parameters, headers, body — which is why that day mattered. Setting up a typical authenticated call: - **Method**: `POST` - **URL**: `https://api.example.com/v1/contacts` - **Authentication**: choose *Generic Credential Type → Header Auth* (or Predefined Credential Type if n8n knows the service). Store the token here, **never** hard-coded in the URL or a header field — credentials in n8n are encrypted and reusable, and they do not leak into exported workflow JSON. - **Send Query Parameters**: on, if you need `?source=website` - **Send Body**: on, Body Content Type `JSON`, then either build fields in the UI or switch to *Using JSON* and write: ```json { "name": "{{ $json.name }}", "email": "{{ $json.email }}", "custom": { "team_size": {{ $json.team_size }} } } ``` Note there are no quotes around the second expression — `team_size` should be a number, and wrapping it in quotes would send a string. That distinction causes real 422 errors. Options worth knowing on the same node: **Pagination** (n8n can follow `next` links or increment a page parameter automatically until results run out), **Batching** (throttle to respect rate limits), **Retry On Fail** with a wait between tries, **Timeout**, **Response → Include Response Headers and Status**, and **Ignore SSL Issues** (use only against internal test servers). A genuinely useful shortcut: most API docs include a `curl` example. Click **Import cURL** in the HTTP Request node, paste it, and n8n fills in the method, URL, headers and body for you. ##### The Code node: when logic outgrows expressions Expressions handle one-liners. The **Code node** handles everything else: reshaping data, complex conditionals, deduplicating, grouping, generating multiple items from one. It has two modes, and the difference matters: - **Run Once for All Items** — your code runs a single time with `items` (all of them) available. Use for aggregating, grouping, deduplicating, sorting. - **Run Once for Each Item** — your code runs per item with `$json` for the current one. Use for simple per-record transformation. A realistic example — cleaning and filtering an API response, all-items mode: ```javascript // Input: raw contacts from an API. Output: cleaned, deduplicated, qualified leads. const seen = new Set(); const results = []; for (const item of $input.all()) { const c = item.json; const email = (c.email_address ?? '').trim().toLowerCase(); if (!email.includes('@')) continue; // drop invalid if (seen.has(email)) continue; // drop duplicates seen.add(email); const size = Number(c.team_size ?? 0); results.push({ json: { full_name: `${c.first_name ?? ''} ${c.last_name ?? ''}`.trim(), email, company: c.org?.name ?? 'Unknown', team_size: size, tier: size >= 50 ? 'enterprise' : size >= 10 ? 'mid' : 'small', synced_at: new Date().toISOString(), }, }); } return results; ``` Three rules for the Code node: 1. **Return an array of objects, each wrapped in `{ json: {...} }`.** Returning a bare object is the most common error. 2. **`return []` means zero items downstream** — a legitimate way to filter everything out. 3. **Python is available** (Pyodide) but runs in a WebAssembly sandbox: slower to start, no arbitrary pip packages. Choose JavaScript unless you specifically need Python. Self-hosted instances can also allow external npm modules via `NODE_FUNCTION_ALLOW_EXTERNAL`, which is another self-hosting advantage. ##### IF and Switch: branching **IF** is two-way. Set conditions (with proper type selection — String, Number, Boolean, DateTime, Array) and the node emits two outputs, `true` and `false`. Wire different node chains to each. Always wire *both*, even if the false branch just goes to a NoOp — an unwired branch silently discards items. **Switch** is many-way. Two modes: *Rules* (define a condition per output, up to many branches, with an optional fallback output) and *Expression* (return an output index from JavaScript). Switch is the right choice for tier routing: ```javascript // Switch node, Expression mode — route by lead tier {{ $json.tier === 'enterprise' ? 0 : $json.tier === 'mid' ? 1 : 2 }} ``` ```mermaid flowchart LR H[HTTP Request:
fetch leads] --> C[Code:
clean + dedupe] C --> S{Switch on tier} S -->|0 enterprise| A[HTTP: create CRM deal] S -->|1 mid| B[Sheets: append row] S -->|2 small| D[Email: nurture] A --> M[Merge] B --> M D --> M M --> L[Sheets: log run] ``` ##### Merge, Set, and item manipulation **Merge** rejoins branches or combines two data sources. Its modes: *Append* (stack items from both inputs), *Combine* by matching field (a join, like SQL), *Combine by position*, and *Combine All* (cross product). The match-field mode is how you enrich: fetch orders from one API, customers from another, and join them on `customer_id`. **Set** (now "Edit Fields") builds a clean output object explicitly. Turn on **Keep Only Set** and you get exactly the fields you defined — nothing else. This is the professional habit: right before writing to a destination, add a Set node that declares precisely the shape you intend to send. It makes workflows self-documenting and prevents accidental leakage of raw API fields. Other item helpers worth knowing: **Split Out** (turn one item's array field into many items — n8n's iterator), **Aggregate** (fold many items into one), **Remove Duplicates**, **Sort**, **Limit**, and **Loop Over Items** for explicit batching. ##### When to use which — the assignment answer - **Built-in node** — first choice whenever it exists. Authentication, pagination and error handling are handled for you, and the workflow is readable by your teammates. *Example: Google Sheets → Append Row.* - **HTTP Request node** — when no built-in node exists, or the built-in node lacks the specific endpoint you need. You control everything and pay for it in configuration. *Example: calling a regional payment gateway's `/settlements` endpoint.* - **Code node** — when the transformation is beyond expressions: multi-step logic, grouping, deduplication, generating N items from 1. *Example: collapsing 200 line items into per-customer totals.* The ordering principle: **built-in > HTTP > code**, always reaching for the simplest option that works, because every step down that list costs future maintainers more effort. ##### Common pitfalls - **Hard-coding API keys** in URLs or headers instead of using credentials — they end up in exported JSON and screenshots. - **Returning the wrong shape from Code** — remember `[{ json: {...} }]`. - **Assuming one item.** Code in per-item mode runs repeatedly; API calls inside a loop can blow through rate limits. - **Ignoring pagination** — you process page 1 and never notice pages 2–40. - **Unwired IF branches** discarding data silently. - **Expressions on missing fields** throwing `Cannot read property of undefined` — use `?.` and `??`. - **Not enabling Retry On Fail** for flaky third-party APIs. ##### Your hands-on tie-in The practical task is the essential rehearsal: use the **HTTP Request node** to call a public API, transform the response in a **Code node** (extract and rename fields), then reference that transformed data downstream with **expressions**. `https://api.github.com/users/torvalds/repos?per_page=10` is a good target — it returns an array, so you immediately face multi-item handling. The mini project is the real deliverable: pull data from an API **with no built-in integration**, filter with an **IF node**, transform kept items in a **Code node**, and write them to a sheet or database. Choose an API nobody has integrated — a public transit feed, a cricket scores API, your college's open data — because the whole point is proving you no longer need permission from an integrations list. Finish with the assignment: a short guide on **when to use a built-in node, the HTTP Request node, or the Code node**, with one example of each. Use the ordering principle above; it is the kind of judgment employers are actually testing for. ##### Key takeaways - Expressions (`{{ }}`) evaluate JavaScript at run time; drag from the Schema view to get paths right and use `?.` / `??` for optional fields. - The HTTP Request node makes every REST API integrable — store credentials properly, use Import cURL, and enable pagination and retries. - The Code node handles logic beyond expressions; return `[{ json: {...} }]` and pick the right all-items vs per-item mode. - IF gives two branches, Switch gives many with a fallback; always wire every branch. - Merge joins data sources, Set declares a clean output shape, and Split Out/Aggregate handle arrays. Prefer built-in > HTTP > code.
